question: EU blade manufacturers have raised serious concerns regarding new import duties and potential anti-dumping measures for specialised carbon steel strips (HS codes 7211290090 / 7211290099) imported from Taiwan and South Korea. These steel strips are essential for the production of razor blades.

However, they have not been produced in the EU for decades, meaning that such measures do not protect any current EU steel production, but instead threaten the survival of downstream manufacturers who depend on this specific input.

One such company exports around 98 % of its production, and the sudden imposition of import duties of approximately 25 % creates a severe and unpredictable financial burden for the company. It undermines contractual stability and risks forcing one of the last remaining EU blade producers out of the market.

While trade defence instruments can be justified where there is EU-based production, the Commission must also ensure that such measures do not unintentionally destroy strategic downstream industries and their supply chains. 1.
Is the Commission considering targeted exemptions or suspension mechanisms for supply-chain inputs that are not made by EU producers, in order to protect downstream manufacturing?

How will the Commission improve transparency and predictability for small and medium-sized enterprises regarding the application and timing of anti-dumping duties in order to prevent retroactive shocks?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.4.2026) An anti-dumping (AD) investigation on cold rolled flat steel products originating, inter alia, in Taiwan, but not from South Korea has been ongoing since 18 September 2025. No measures have been imposed in that investigation.

However, a 25% import duty is applicable to imports of the product category (HS code 72112900) from Taiwan under the EU’s steel safeguard measure as the duty-free quota for Taiwan was fully utilised for the first quarter of 2026. For South Korea, the duty-free quota for the first quarter of 2026 has not yet been fully utilised. Only imports above the quota attract a duty.

In safeguard investigations, users’ interests are taken into account, and measures in the form of a tariff rate quota allow a certain volume to be imported duty free so that downstream users are not unduly penalised. Data on the quota usage is publicly available on the website of Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union1.

The order numbers for the product category are given in the updated version of the Safeguard Regulation2. In AD investigations, the Commission also conducts an EU interest test to see if measures would be against the EU interest, including the impact on downstream users. The decision on EU interest relies on information submitted by interested parties, including users. The procedures are set out in Section 5.

5 of the Notice of Initiation3. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the Commission reaches out to increase awareness through regular engagement with the SME community. Directorate-General for Trade and Economic Security (DG TRADE) also has a dedicated webpage4 for SMEs regarding trade defence.
Finally, DG TRADE’s information page on each ongoing investigation5 indicates the timetable for the steps in a proceeding.
